A.explanation: The external circuit receives only $VQ$, where $V$ is the terminal p.d., which is less than $E$ when the cell has internal resistance.

B.explanation: Only part of the total energy is dissipated inside the cell as $(E-V)Q$, not the full energy $EQ$ supplied by the cell.

C.explanation: The product $EQ$ has units of joules and is an energy, so it cannot equal a resistance measured in ohms.

D.explanation: The e.m.f. $E$ is the total energy supplied per unit charge, so for charge $Q$ the total energy dissipated in both places is $EQ$.

hints: Recall what e.m.f. $E$ means: energy supplied by the cell per unit charge $Q$ passing through it, compared with terminal p.d. $V$ across the external circuit only.
Write the defining relation $E = W/Q$ and rearrange to $W = EQ$, then ask where that total energy $W$ ends up when current flows.
Split the total into internal dissipation plus external dissipation and check which option describes the whole $EQ$ and which describes only $VQ$; also check the units of $EQ$ against resistance.
walkthrough: Start from the definition: e.m.f. $E$ is the electrical energy supplied by the cell per unit charge that passes through the cell, so $E = W/Q$.
Rearrange to $W = EQ$: when charge $Q$ is delivered, the cell supplies total energy $EQ$ in joules.
By conservation of energy this total must be dissipated in two places: as heat inside the cell due to internal resistance plus as energy dissipated in the external resistors.
The external part alone is $VQ$, where $V$ is the terminal p.d., and the internal part alone is $(E - V)Q$, so neither alone equals $EQ$ unless internal resistance is zero.
Also $EQ$ cannot be a resistance because $\text{V} \times \text{C} = \text{J}$, an energy unit, not ohms.
Therefore the statement that the total energy dissipated in the cell and the external circuit is $EQ$ follows directly. This is option D.
